newsitem.title: USA: Scandals loom in Clinton's second term.
newsitem.headline: Scandals loom in Clinton's second term.

text.p: Now that President Bill Clinton has navigated the turbulent rapids of re-election, he heads into still-swirling ethical waters, hoping to avoid the second term fate of some of his predecessors.

The latest entry on Clinton's scandal sheet -- questions about Democratic campaign financing -- gave Republican Bob Dole and Reform Party nominee Ross Perot a new opening to attack the president's ethics and character in the weeks just before Tuesday's election.

Critics asked whether the Clinton administration had peddled access and influence in exchange for hefty campaign contributions from wealthy Asian interests. But the questions have not ended with the election. They may be just beginning.

Senate Republican leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said Wednesday the newly-elected Congress will hold hearings on the Democrats' campaign finances. "The Congress has the responsiblity to at least look into some of these matters ... I'm sure we'll have some hearings," Lott said.

That would be in addition to a multitude of congressional hearings that have already been held and three investigations underway by independent counsels probing the activities of Clinton, his wife, and his aides and associates.

For Clinton, the list of still unresolved issues seems endless -- from the Whitewater land deal he and his wife Hillary invested in years ago to questions about possible obstruction of justice by people in his White House.

The New York Times warned Wednesday that Clinton must clean house if necessary and cooperate with legitimate inquiries "if he wants to avoid being remembered simply as the most investigated President in the modern era."
There have been other, even more dire, predictions about Clinton's future.
"We are headed toward a second Watergate with all this stuff going on and a constitutional crisis in 1997," was the blunt assessment of Texas billionaire and third party candidate Perot.

Recent history offers little comfort for Clinton, even if he is the first Democrat to win re-election to the White House in decades. The last two Republicans who won second terms found it did not save them from major legal headaches.

Richard Nixon went from the glory of an Election Day victory to the humiliation of the Watergate scandal, which made him the first president forced to resign in disgrace. Ronald Reagan spent the latter half of his second term trying to explain and avoid the blame from the Iran-Contra affair.

During Clinton's first term, Kenneth Starr, the special Whitewater prosecutor, has seen his mission grow from Whitewater itself to include the firing of the White House Travel Office staff in 1993 and the request by Clinton aides for confidential FBI background files on hundreds of people, many of them prominent Republicans.

Although Starr's office is tight-lipped about its probe, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton has been forced to testify before a grand jury -- creating the extraordinary but not impossible scenario that she could face a federal indictment.

Mrs Clinton insists she knows nothing about once-missing billing records from her days with the Rose Law firm in Arkansas. Those records, long sought by federal investigators, turned up suddenly in the White House private quarters.
Independent counsels also are looking into the actions of Housing Secretary Henry Cisneros and former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.
In a move to reduce direct political pressure on such probes, independent counsels operate free of funding worries -- no matter what party controls the White House or Congress.
The rise of special prosecutors stems from the Watergate era and a bid to reassure an angry public that a dependable apparatus was in place to monitor the government.

The most devastating political scandal in American history began in the midst of the 1972 election year, when Nixon re-election campaign operatives broke into opposition Democratic Party headquarters in Washington's Watergate complex and were caught red-handed.

But over the next two years, inquiries pressed first by a judge and The Washington Post and then by Congress and prosecutors unravelled a bewildering web of political crimes that led finally to the Oval Office itself.

Ronald Reagan also knew the joy of a re-election victory. In 1984 he scored the biggest landslide in U.S. history, winning 525 of a possible 538 votes in the Electoral College and sweeping 49 of 50 states against Democrat Walter Mondale.

But by 1986 he was thrust into crisis when it was disclosed that his administration had sold arms to Iran in 1985-86 and diverted the proceeds to Contra rebels in Nicaragua -- defying a congressional ban on such funding.
